newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia summons Singapore envoy over merger tiff.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia summons Singapore envoy over merger tiff.

text.p: Malaysia, caught in a verbal row with Singapore over the question of possible reunification, on Monday summoned Singapore's top envoy and expressed its displeasure with the city state's handling of the issue.

Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi called High Commissioner Low Choon Ming to his office to tell him that Malaysian leaders were offended by Singapore's actions, the national Bernama news agency said.
Abdullah said he later telephoned his Singaporean counterpart, S. Jayakumar, to further express Malaysia's feelings on the issue.
Singapore Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew touched off a debate about the possibility of Singapore again becoming a part of Malaysia, as it was from 1963 to 1965, during a speech in June.
Comments by Lee that a re-merger could happen if Malaysia ended its policy of giving special rights to indigenous races and pursued meritocracy stirred controversy in both countries.

Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, speaking for his United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), on Saturday said that statements by Singapore leaders on the merger issue had offended his party.
"They are only trying to show that Malaysia is bad and did not practise meritocracy, and that Singaporeans will be punished if they did not perform," said Mahathir, the president of UMNO.
He said UMNO was "deeply saddened" that it had to criticize Singapore.
"But we are offended by their recent statements, which are insincere," he said. "They are using us as the bogeyman to scare Singaporeans."
A public opinion poll by Singapore Straits Times newspaper recently showed many Singaporeans opposed reunification.
Abdullah said UMNO's supreme council felt that the statements by Singapore's leaders constituted "a criticism of the internal affairs of a country."

Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong, reacting to Mahathir's statement, said there was no need to use Malaysia as a "bogeyman" to frighten voters into supporting Singapore's ruling People's Action Party.
"If we have to use Malaysia to campaign as a bogeyman, that will have no effect," the Straits Times quoted Goh as saying.
Goh, who is expected to call a general election soon, said the issues were more mundane like the cost of living, health care, car prices and the upgrading of housing.
